claims.text: Corrosion protection of Q235 steel during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C is governed by the quality and continuity of its native iron-oxide film.
A uniform, adherent oxide layer forming along pre-existing grain boundaries delays corrosion by limiting oxygen and salt-ion diffusion.
Heterogeneous grain-boundary distributions cause defective oxide coverage, localized scale breakdown, and accelerated corrosion.
As-received Q235 steel has minimal pre-formed protective scale.
Controlled annealing can homogenize the grain-boundary distribution of Q235 steel.
Annealing-induced grain-boundary homogenization promotes more uniform in-situ oxide formation.
Oxidation kinetics at 700–900 °C are sufficient to produce a protective scale during molten Na2SO4/NaCl exposure.
Room-temperature oxidation is too slow to form a protective scale over the same exposure duration.
The relevant Q235 oxide scale is expected to contain Fe2O3 and/or Fe3O4.
Elevated temperature accelerates oxidation and produces a thicker oxide film.
Uniformly distributed grain boundaries favor formation of a continuous and adherent oxide film.
A continuous and adherent oxide film reduces subsequent ionic diffusion and corrosion.
Poorly connected grain boundaries produce defective oxide films that undergo spallation and localized accelerated corrosion.
Annealed Q235 specimens will develop a more uniform and adherent oxide film than as-received specimens during salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
Annealed Q235 specimens will exhibit lower net mass change and less spallation than as-received specimens during salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
At room temperature, annealed and untreated Q235 specimens will exhibit similarly minimal oxide formation and similar corrosion responses.
Intentional alloying can substantially alter oxide or corrosion-product formation behavior, limiting transfer of the proposed mechanism to other alloys.

contradictions.description: The governing film is called a native oxide film, implying a pre-existing film, while the initial state specifies minimal pre-formed scale and the mediator/mechanism primarily describe an oxide layer that forms during high-temperature exposure. It is therefore unclear whether protection is attributed to the pre-exposure native film or to the subsequently grown scale.
